title: Organs, guitars and drums

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymnals: what a church believes, carried home in song. Your line was theology in song.

The first note comes up through the floor before it reaches your ears: a low hum in your shoes, then a stone room filled with sound from a wall of metal pipes. Across town, a drummer clicks his sticks, one, two, three, four, and a guitar and a bass come in under a screen of lyrics. In a third church, there's no instrument at all. A single voice sings a line, and the room answers it. Ask in any of those rooms what's going on, and you may hear the same answer: praising God with what they have.

Start at the end of the Psalms. Psalm one hundred fifty is a list of instruments, and the King James Bible says: "Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs." Organs, right there. But some readers take the Hebrew word behind it as a simple pipe, nothing like a cathedral organ with pedals. The psalm was gathering every sound it knew. Next, the new. Another psalm says: "Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise." Churches with guitars, drums and keyboards often point to lines like that. So do churches with pipe organs, which were once new themselves. Each generation brings the instruments it has. Then, the churches that use none. Orthodox churches traditionally sing their services without instruments, and so do some Protestant churches, such as the Churches of Christ. They read Paul's words to the Ephesians: "singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord." For them, the human voice is the instrument God made. Each of these churches has reasons, and takes them seriously. Last, the end of that list psalm. After trumpet, harp, strings, pipes and two kinds of cymbal, it doesn't end on an instrument: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Every instrument on the list depends on breath, and every person has it.

Play a recording of an organ, a gospel band or a hymn with guitar, and listen for two minutes, noticing where the sound sits in your body: chest, feet, throat. If you can't play anything, listen to your own breathing, the instrument the psalm ends on. If you pray, you can let the music carry your prayer without words; if you don't, just listen all the way to the end.
Organs. The pipes in old churches, a word the King James Psalms already used, and a reminder that churches praise with the sounds they have.
Your line: every instrument praise. The week ran from colors of the year, incense and candles to the cross, icons, hymnals and organs: faith you can see, smell and hear. That's the week.

notes: Editor pass: the lexical claim about the Hebrew behind 'organs' is now 'some readers take it as a pipe' (no 'probably' or 'uncertain' as fact), Orthodox unaccompanied singing is 'traditionally', and the hook's 'three rooms, three sounds' line (a device used on days 1356 and 1358) was rewritten.

The Hebrew ugav (עוּגָב) in Psalm 150:4, rendered 'organs' in the KJV, is generally taken as a pipe or flute; the lesson says 'probably' and 'uncertain'. Confirm, and confirm the Hebrew spelling and pronunciation.
'Organs' is the index word (title head); the lesson spans organs, guitars and drums as the title does.
'Pipe organs, which were once new themselves' is a general historical remark without a date; confirm acceptable.
Orthodox churches singing unaccompanied, and the Churches of Christ as an example of Protestant a cappella worship: confirm fair description.
